title: Current Position | Weekly Briefing November 11th to November 17th [PODCAST]
summary: Recent U.S. flight disruptions underscore the need for shippers to enhance resilience through scenario planning and coordination with service providers.
body_markdown:
Recent flight disruptions in the U.S. are highlighting how quickly unexpected events can impact air cargo capacity and the flow of critical shipments. As global supply chains face continued pressure from operational and geopolitical challenges, scenario planning, close coordination with service providers, and building greater resilience are becoming increasingly important for shippers preparing for what comes next.


• 14 min


Current Position | Weekly Briefing November 11th - 17th


The Expeditors Podcast


Play


**


You're listening to Current Position, a weekly briefing from Expeditors mapping the shifts across trade compliance, regulatory changes, and global supply chains. Plus, some market insights from our Senior Vice President of Global Air, Karl Francisco.


I'm Chris Parker, and here's the latest from November 11th to November 17th.


**Global Customs & Trade Market**


-


The USTR has extended all 178 Section 301 China exclusions to Jan. 9, 2027. The exclusions covering items such as chemicals, certain electronics and medical equipment were due to lapse Nov. 9. They now remain valid through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Jan. 9, 2027, under a Federal Register Notice published Nov. 10.


[Read more](https://info.expeditors.com/newsflash/ustr-announces-section-301-exclusion-extension?hsLang=en-us) .


-


EU officials plan to launch official deforestation rules on December 30 that will impact importers and exporters of certain timber products. These new EUDR requirements will require certain timber operators to file a Due Diligence Statement through the EUDR Information System before goods are sold in or exported from the EU. The commission advises businesses to review supply chains to avoid potential shipment delays.[Read more](https://info.expeditors.com/newsflash/eu-introduces-new-requirements-for-deforestation-regulation?hsLang=en-us) .


Global Ocean Market


-


More services continue to return to routes via the Suez Canal. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd plan to move three more Gemini services - AE2, AE3 and AE1 - from the Cape of Good Hope route to Suez transits. The services will begin following the routes in mid-December and into early January 2027. Both carriers said further network changes depend on continued stability in the Red Sea.[Read more](https://gcaptain.com/maersk-hapag-lloyd-expand-suez-canal-return-with-three-more-gemini-services/) .


-


Panama Canal authorities lift daily capacity to 34 transits. An added Super-category booking slot at the Panamax locks takes that allocation from 18 to 19 and total daily capacity to 34 slots. The maximum Neopanamax draft was also increased to 15.24 meters or 50 feet from November 9. Authorities said the changes were able to be made thanks to improved lake levels.[Read more](https://www.ajot.com/news/panama-canal-increases-daily-transits-to-34-and-raises-maximum-allowable-draft-at-neopanamax-locks) .


-


U.S. container imports hit a record 2.67 million TEUs in October. Volumes rose 16% from a year earlier, with China-origin cargo reaching just shy of 988,000 TEUs. U.S. East and Gulf Coast ports all gained market share. Average transit delays also rose to 6.3 days, up from 4.2 days in June, according to Descartes. Contract talks continue with ILWU-represented watchmen at Los Angeles and Long Beach. Employers warn a strike could affect terminals handling more than half of the two ports' combined cargo.[Read more](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/u-s-container-imports-hit-record-2-67-million-teus-in-october-as-port-delays-rise) .


Global Air Market


-


U.S. air cargo operations are recovering quickly following a temporary ground stop of all flights across the U.S. last week. The stoppage resulted in many delayed flights as the Federal Aviation Administration had concerns over a telecommunications systems failure. The U.S. Congress allocated $12.5 billion to upgrade communications infrastructure in 2025, but that work has not been completed.[Read more](https://www.aircargonews.net/cargo-airport/2026/11/us-air-cargo-supply-chains-recover-following-ground-stop/) .


-


Air cargo rates increased 2% earlier this month as volumes softened ahead of peak. WorldACD's global average reached $3.45 in week 45, 31% above a year ago, while worldwide chargeable weight slipped 2%. China-to-Europe tonnage was down 13% year on year, and Hong Kong-to-Europe volumes were 32% lower. This decline has been seen since the EU changed its import rules in July. Taiwan's AI-related exports lifted volumes to the U.S. by 7%.[Read more](https://www.ajot.com/news/worldacd-weekly-air-cargo-trends-week-45-2026) .


Global Ground Transport Market


-


European road freight rates hit record highs in Q3 even as volumes fell. The contract index rose to 148.9 points and the spot index to 147.6, both series highs. Volume on main corridors, meanwhile, fell 4.5% quarter on quarter. Diesel, averaging €2.05 per litre, squeezed hauliers' margins on several lanes.[Read more](https://trans.info/en/road-freight-rates-q3-2026-record-513960) .


-


U.S. spot van rates edge up to $3.11 per mile. DAT's weekly report shows the van spot rate in the U.S. rose 4 cents November 7-13. During that same week, truck posts climbed 9% while load posts fell 6%. Van linehaul rates remain 36% above a year earlier. DAT analysts expect year-over-year gains to narrow after Thanksgiving.[Read more](https://www.ajot.com/news/dat-spot-truckload-market-report-nov-7-13-week-46) .


-


Chilean truckers last week set up blockades of roads over diesel prices. Strikes and blockades disrupted the north-south highway and access to ports including Iquique. Protesters were demanding measures to contain and stabilize fuel prices. The government plans a bill to prevent weekly fuel price increases of more than 20 pesos per liter.[Read more](https://www.ajot.com/news/truckers-block-roads-in-chile-protesting-fuel-price-hikes) .


Up next, Senior Vice President of Global Air, Karl Francisco.


*The following discussion could include forward-looking statements. Of course, actual results may differ materially because of various risks and uncertainties. We are not obligated to update these statements, and we rarely do so. Instead, we refer you to our most recent SEC filings for more information about the risk factors that could affect our future results.*


Chris Parker:


Mr. Francisco, welcome to this week's Current Position. What is on your mind? And I guess I'm gonna, I'm gonna assume that it's one particular thing that happened last week. Let's talk about it.


Karl Francisco:


Yeah, glad to be here again, Chris. Happy to be here, quite honestly. You know, over the, over the... I think I mentioned to you on my last call that I travel a lot, and I was on the road again last week. Uh, I, I think over the last perhaps six weeks, I've probably been to 12 different countries, meeting with airlines, all of our global carriers, meeting with, uh, shippers as well. Uh, the purpose of the meetings was really to get a really good idea of what can we expect for the rest of this year in terms of where we see the marketplace, as well as where we think, uh, 27. is going to land in terms of capacity, demand- Cost and so on. So got a real good feel for what might happen next year based on our meetings with the airlines.


But what's top of mind was on my way home from, uh, from Turkiye, um, uh, my phone started lighting up about what's going on in the United States with the FAA grounding a lot of flights. For a short period of time, there was, I think, close to 9,000 flights that were canceled or grounded. So the first thing that came to mind was, okay, hopefully I can land so I can get home. Okay. And then I started thinking about, okay, what's next? There's a lot of people thinking about how to be at home. They're stranded. And ob-obviously, you know, the next thing that comes to mind is cargo for me. Um, and how will customers start, you know, shipping cargo again? What do we do, uh, if the flights are grounded in the US? Is that happening anywhere else in the world? That's the first thing that came to mind. And then if it's only in the US, what do we do? How do we get cargo in and out of the US now? That, that was a big issue and something that I, I thought about a lot.


Chris Parker:


Yeah. I want to ask, you've landed, um, your phone is blowing up with notifications. What are the kinds of things that get asked of you as Senior Vice President of Global Air for a forwarder when it comes to situations like this?


Karl Francisco:


Yeah. Well, you know, the first thing is, you know, they want to learn as much as they can about what happened, what took place, what can we expect, what do you hear from the carriers? So I started, uh, you know, communicating with a lot of our global carriers, and they were really gracious and generous to let me know what was going on in their part of the world, uh, as well as what was going on in the US since it was, it happened to be the, in the US only.


So that was a relief. And, um, because it's so fresh and so new, you know, um, you can only get so much information rather quickly. So it, it's really, you know, being close with the airlines, being close with what's happening on the ground, and trying to convey as much information as you can to as many people as you can about what to expect. Okay. And again, I, I think the number one concern was, you know, if we can't get cargo out, then what do we do? Or if we can't get cargo into the country, what do we do, right? And it's one thing, you know, not being able to make your quarter, you know, if you're a retailer, what have you.


And, and that's, that's not a good thing. But, you know, when you start thinking about, you know, some of the more crucial things that's being shipped, like, you know, healthcare and things that save people's lives, that's the first thing that comes to mind, like, what do we do? How do we get these products to customers so that they could, you know, utilize these products?


Chris Parker:


So there have been disruptions like this in the past, right? Um, whether it comes to just the US or just other regions. What is the, I guess, the order of operations for a forwarder when it comes to situations like that? And then what do we actually have control over or, or influence over?


Karl Francisco:


Yeah. You, you know, if you look back, you know, going back to, uh, COVID until today, we've experienced so many disruptions in the industry, you know, not only with air freight and ocean freight, what have you, but it's just coming at us left and right, um, and you really have to be prepared.


Um, and, you know, when you think about the transportation industry, it operates through a highly synchronized network of airlines, terminal operators, transit systems, uh, data, employees. You know, when something happens and it takes things off schedule, it becomes a, a real big problem to get it back on schedule. And depending on how long the problem occurs, it could take weeks to get back to normal. So that's the first thing that comes to mind. And, you know, in working with a lot of customers, what I find is some of the more ex- you know, experienced customers that's been through a lot of this, what I find is they have one thing in common, uh, that, um, you know, they have to know how to deal with these disruptions. And the best way to deal with it is they create scenario planning. Okay. What does that mean?


It means that they're working with their providers, um, getting them in a room and looking at what ifs, all of the what ifs. What happens if you can't ship to this location anymore? What do we do? And you start working through it, and it takes time, but you have to be prepared and start thinking about all of the people on the supply chain and be ready when something like this happens, you know, uh, in the US. So I, I think my recommendation would be for a lot of companies to start thinking about, you know, what happens, you know, if we have another event that affects my business and I can't ship products anymore? What do I do, right? And making sure that you have everyone in the supply chain on your team working through scenario planning and coming up with the best way to solve these problems is probably the best thing you can do right now.


Chris Parker:


What is driving such tight integration within the supply chain transportation ecosystem? I mean, it sounds like there's so many dependencies on various legs of a, of a journey. It's both a blessing and a curse, right? It's great because it's, it can be efficient, but when things like this happen, there's some major challenges and just the synchronicity is, is thrown off. Where's all that coming from?


Karl Francisco:


Well, I, I think if you look back again over the last, you know, four years, you know, with all of the, the changes that took place in, in the industry, you know, when it comes to geopolitical issues, you know, the, the conflict in the Middle East, it's really creating a lot of problems with customers trying to get their product to market.


All they're thinking about doing now is speeding it up, having a more consistent, reliable supply chain. And it's challenging because you're faced with all of these issues on a monthly, weekly basis now that, um, there's not a lot of time to think about these things, and you have to start thinking about how do we build more resilience in the supply chain, right? Because it's moving very fast right now.


Chris Parker:


Any other thoughts regarding the, uh, the events from last week and, and anything that's transpired since then?


Karl Francisco:


You know, after going through what we went through in the US last week, you know, it's a good idea to start reaching out to a lot of customers and a lot of service providers in the industry to get together and start thinking about, you know, what if? What happens if this happens again in the future? What can we do to, to help one another, to help the customers get their products to market? Uh, I think that's really important.


And I think everyone's moving so quickly right now, you know, to get shipments moving, we're not really thinking ahead. We're not really thinking about, you know, uh, you know, six months from now or a year from now or even longer. And I, I think we need to start looking at that because that's really the only way you can, uh, really improve the supply chain, in my, my opinion.


Chris Parker:


What else would you say customers, clients are thinking about when it comes to scenario planning, and what should they be asking of their providers?


Karl Francisco:


You know, things are moving a lot, you know, moving manufacturing from one country to another country. Uh, when that happens, please reach out to your service providers and include them so that they're prepared for it. We're seeing more disruption around the world, you know, with airlines and terminals being overwhelmed with the amount of cargo and the amount of demand that, that they're seeing right now.


Uh, and we're seeing it a lot. It's really brittle in, in certain locations. So when something like this happens, if something changes in the supply chain, you know, please notify your service provider so that they can work with you and, and be prepared to handle that, that change in your supply chain.


Chris Parker:


What's helping you get out of bed these days, Karl?


Karl Francisco:


Um, moving shipments and making sure that they get to the customers as quickly as possible.


Chris Parker:


Happy customers. That's the key.


Karl Francisco:


That's all I worry about.


Chris Parker:


Well, thanks so much for the time, Karl.


Karl Francisco:


All right. Thank you, Chris.


You are now at our current position. Links to everything we covered today, plus some extra articles of interest, are in the show notes.


And while you're there, check out the events and webinars we flagged for the weeks ahead. Thank you for listening, and we'll see you next week.
